turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this screen is taking forever to load. What brought you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): My daughter insisted. I slid down a couple times, but I didn't really fall. My knees just kind of went.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mom, you were on the kitchen floor both times. I found you by the fridge on Tuesday, and you were shaky.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): I slid. That linoleum is from 1987 and it's slick if you've got socks on. I've been meaning to replace it for ages.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on, the chart just jumped. Can you say again how many times this happened?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Twice. Once around last week and once a few days ago. Not falls, though. I just ended up sitting down.
[SEG0007] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): First one was about ten days ago, second was Tuesday. And she gets dizzy every time she stands up. She grabs the counter and won't admit how bad it is.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's a little lightheaded for a second, then it passes. I've had that for years, sort of, if I pop up too fast.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. The nurse already did lying and standing pressures. Lying was 158 over 86, pulse 68. Standing, after a minute, 122 over 74, pulse 84.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that terrible? My sister's pressure runs low, but she doesn't take blood pressure pills. She takes biotin every morning for her hair.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Biotin isn't part of this. What medicines do you actually take? The list on here is a mess.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure ones. Lisinopril ten milligrams in the morning, amlodipine five milligrams, and the water pill, hydrochlorothiazide twenty-five. Plus zolpidem five milligrams at bedtime so I can sleep. The neighbor's dog barks half the night, have I mentioned that?
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say the sleeping pill again? I was clicking the wrong tab.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Zolpidem, five milligrams, at bedtime. Couple of years now.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You forgot the metoprolol, Mom. Twenty-five milligrams morning and night. They added it last year.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, right, I do take the metoprolol. Twenty-five twice a day. I lump it in with the others.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): So lisinopril 10 daily, amlodipine 5, hydrochlorothiazide 25, metoprolol 25 twice a day, zolpidem 5 at night. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. Penicillin made me itchy when I was a kid, so I've stayed away from it ever since. Nothing else.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll keep penicillin on the list. Any chest pain, or shortness of breath, or blacking out with these slides?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, no trouble breathing, and I never blacked out. I knew right where I was. My cherry tomatoes are coming in early, by the way, if you like tomatoes.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She didn't hit her head either time. Just sat down hard and looked pale.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Screen froze again. Did she hit her head or not?
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. No head injury. She was just shaky afterward.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): And no bad headaches lately. I get one now and then but not with this.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me listen a second. Heart is regular, no murmur. Lungs are clear.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. I live by myself, you know, except my daughter pops in most evenings. The dog next door is the real problem.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I check on her after work. She minimizes everything. Those two times she was fully on the floor.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think this is your pressure dropping when you stand, with the slides from that. The water pill is likely making it worse.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I stop something? I hate changing pills. Last time they changed one I felt funny for a week.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm stopping the hydrochlorothiazide. Don't take any more of the twenty-five milligram water pill, starting today.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure the bottle comes out of her kitchen drawer.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. Keep the others the same? The zolpidem too? I really can't sleep without it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, leave the lisinopril, amlodipine, metoprolol, and zolpidem as they are for now.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): And when I stand up, just go slow, I suppose. I already hold the counter.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Sit on the edge of the bed, count to twenty, then stand. If you feel the spin, sit back down. Don't fight it.
[SEG0036] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll put a chair by the fridge so she has somewhere to land.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might do a head scan if the dizziness does not settle. Not ordering one today.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want a scan unless I have to. Machines and I don't get along. Reminds me of when they redid the kitchen in ninety-eight.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Understood. Let's see you back in two weeks and recheck the standing pressure then.
[SEG0040] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I can bring her. Mornings are better, before she gets tired.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks is fine. Should I call sooner if I slide again?
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you actually pass out, or you fall and can't get up, go to the emergency room. Otherwise I'll see you in two weeks.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. And tell your nurse thank you for the blood pressure, even if the numbers were annoying.

spec.situation: Older patient who fell twice 'but not really fell, slid down'; dizzy on standing; takes several BP and sleeping tablets; daughter reports what the patient minimises; nurse reads lying and standing BP; doctor changes one tablet.
features: hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
